article.title: War on Migrants
article.author: Kate Morrissey
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Human rights monitors from across the Americas met twice in Mexico earlier this year to hold a people’s tribunal over aggressive actions committed by the United States under the Trump administration. On Thursday, the jury from that tribunal announced its preliminary findings during a press conference in Mexico City, with some participants joining virtually from as far away as Brazil. Based on testimony and evidence from more than 50 cases heard over four days, ranging from military attacks on fishing boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean to deportations of immigrants to countries where they do not have ties , the group roundly condemned the United States’ human rights violations and called on international organizations — including the United Nations and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights — to launch investigations. “There’s an overwhelming number of cases and issues that are presented there, but from the most local to the more global geopolitical issues that are at stake, we see this common thread of breaking with the rule of law in an advanced stage of capitalism that requires, for its own survival, intensification of looting and land grabs and violation of rights and extermination and even ecocide and genocide of certain populations,” said Laura Carlsen, director of MIRA: Feminisms and Democracies, in a call with Capital & Main. The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment from Capital & Main. “All illegal aliens receive full due process and have their claims heard,” said Lauren Bis, a spokesperson for the White House. “No lawbreakers in the history of human civilization have been treated better than illegal aliens.” The tribunal, co-founded about 16 years ago by roughly a half-dozen people from several countries and known as Tribunal Internacional de Conciencia de los Pueblos en Movimiento, or International Tribunal of Conscience of Peoples in Movement , met in Ciudad Juarez, Mexico, in September and in Mexico City in October after a series of pre-hearings in several countries including Colombia and the U.S. Camilo Pérez-Bustillo, co-founder of Witness at the Border and of the tribunal, explained that the people’s tribunal traces back to a tribunal organized in 1967 by acclaimed philosophers and writers Bertrand Russell and Jean-Paul Sartre to examine war crimes committed during the Vietnam War. That tribunal took its inspiration from the Nuremberg Trials that prosecuted Nazi officials after World War II, Pérez-Bustillo said. A similar, international tribunal has operated in Italy since the late 1970s. Related: Los Angeles Leads the Nation in Reported ICE Enforcement Incidents “The first commitment of the tribunal is to center the victim in the process,” José Antonio Foronda Farro, an attorney who is leading the jury’s legal review process and co-founded the tribunal, said in Spanish during Thursday’s press conference. Foronda Farro, who specializes in human rights, migration and environmental law, said one of the tribunal’s goals is to be able to denounce the human rights violations it has documented before international organizations, including the United Nations and international courts that hear human rights cases. He said the people’s tribunal itself doesn’t have any sentencing power over the government officials that it is judging, but he still sees the practice as worthwhile. “It’s good to make it visible,” Foronda Farro said in an interview with Capital & Main. “It’s good to spread it.” He said he sees the people’s tribunal as a process rather than an event and emphasized that even the conclusions that the group will share in December won’t be truly final because of the ongoing witnessing, documenting and listening the group will be doing. Carlsen, who participated on the jury, said beyond examining rights violations and broken laws, the tribunal is also looking at what it sees as the impunity that the U.S. government and its officials operate with. “We have seen this leading to a level of dispossession, disappearance, discrimination and displacement, among many other crimes — many against humanity — and that we have not seen in other moments in history,” Carlsen said in Spanish during the press conference. Julio Moreira, professor of sociology and law at Universidade Federal da Integração Latino-Americana in Foz do Iguaçu, Brazil, said he was particularly concerned about the U.S. government’s attempts to meddle in other countries’ elections, including in Brazil and Honduras. “We are connected to political issues in a way that isn’t tied to any specific partisan politics,” Moreira said in Spanish. “Rather, it is a politics of humanity.” Related: He Won Protection From Torture: Then ICE Deported Him to Mexico The jury will release a final report in December that will include a specific review of individual international laws and conventions it said was broken by the U.S. government. In the meantime, the preliminary findings provide a resounding indictment of the Trump administration’s policies and practices. The jury organized its findings around four themes — genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity; neofascism and U.S. intervention; migrant genocide and carceral imperialism; and environmental justice and ecocide. “In the United States, migrant people are assassinated and persecuted, creating a regime of terror that reaches even U.S. citizens who dare to intervene in the arbitrary detention of migrants,” the report says. In addition, the jury writes in the report that the U.S. also promotes similar policies in other countries, such as Mexico’s use of its National Guard to block migrants heading north. It says that throughout the hemisphere, migrants are treated as criminals, and their rights are taken away — even their right to life. According to the report, the testimony and evidence that the jury received regarding migration practices included information about unaccompanied migrant children, Indigenous migrants, forced displacement, mass deportation, Haitians stuck at the border in Tijuana, migrants living in a camp in Mexico City and deportation flights to Brazil. The final report will include more specific details from the cases, Carlsen said. The report says that migrants experience different types of economic exploitation on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border, noting that many immigration detention facilities are run by private companies. As of January 2025, nearly 90% of people in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody were in facilities run by private prisons, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse , which gathers and analyzes government data. The U.S. government often transfers people in immigration custody to detention centers far away from their families, friends and lawyers, making it more difficult for them to fight their cases, according to the report. “The United States expands the carceral system as a form of torture to dehumanize migrants,” the report says. It says that deportations occur without following a legal process and that the U.S. government doesn’t necessarily deport people to their countries of origin, but rather to other places. Related: Trump Deports Immigrants to Countries the U.S. Says Are Unsafe It calls out what it says is the racism, xenophobia and discrimination involved in these policies as detrimental to the mental and physical well-being of migrants by exposing them to violence, isolating them and breaking up family and other social ties. The report notes that many groups, including U.S. citizens creating networks to protect Latino migrants, cross-border legal defense networks, shelters and sanctuary cities, are resisting the Trump administration’s policies and trying to support migrants both in the U.S. and abroad. The report calls for protection of migrants’ rights to mobility and for the U.S. to stop considering migration a crime. It urges the U.S. to implement a right to refuge and asylum and guarantee migrants’ rights to health, food, education and work. It calls for an end to attacks, persecution and torture of migrants and human rights defenders as well as to arbitrary detentions and deportations. It says the U.S. should end third country agreements and close detention centers. The report calls on the U.S. to guarantee the return of essential documents to migrants, which, the jury learned during testimony, often does not happen. And, the report says the U.S. should guarantee the right to truth, justice and reparations for the victims of the country’s harmful policies. Elena Gutiérrez, from Movimiento de los Pueblos por la Paz con Justicia, or Movement of the Peoples for Peace and Justice , and Global Exchange called on people in the U.S., Mexico, Canada and the whole of Latin America to organize across borders to defend human rights. The group will present its final report in different locations throughout December, beginning in Mexico City on Dec. 9, the anniversary of the U.N. adopting the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide , and ending in New York in front of the United Nations on Dec. 18, International Migrants Day . Related: She Came to America Seeking Refuge. Now She Fears for Her Life in ICE Detention In a call with Witness at the Border members earlier last week, Pérez-Bustillo pointed out that Dec. 10 is Human Rights Day . “It was the same body of human beings who were thinking about the same issues, who had sort of the same questions in mind that adopted the Genocide Convention one day, and the next day adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, so we want to think about those two instruments and what they represent and sort of the thinking that went into them in a convergent way,” Pérez-Bustillo said. “And that’s the grounding from which the tribunal emerges.” Capital & Main
